title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether using ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool improves academic writing skills among ESL undergraduate students. The author positions the study as an early empirical test of generative AI for writing instruction, addressing the lack of intervention-based evidence on ChatGPT’s effects on writing quality. The research asks whether, when instructional time and tasks are held constant, ChatGPT-supported feedback leads to significantly better writing outcomes than comparison instruction, and how students perceive its impact.

The study used a mixed-methods intervention design with quantitative and qualitative components. Two sections of first-year science and engineering students at a private university in India served as the experimental and comparison groups. The experimental group received a short training session on using ChatGPT for self-assessment and peer-assessment, then used ChatGPT during six hours of instruction on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph writing. ChatGPT was used to support brainstorming, idea development, checking genre features, and feedback on content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary. The comparison group received instruction without this ChatGPT-supported feedback process. Writing performance was measured with pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test tasks scored using validated rubrics; focus group discussions captured student perceptions.

The final analytic sample included 35 students in the experimental group and 37 in the comparison group, all aged 18–19 and studying in English-medium higher education. The setting was a university classroom in India, not a K-12 context. Quantitative results showed statistically significant gains for the experimental group across time and significantly higher post-test and delayed post-test scores than the comparison group. Qualitative findings indicated that students viewed ChatGPT positively for helping with idea generation, staying on topic, organization, grammar explanations, and faster writing, although some also worried about dependence on the tool and reduced creativity.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can function effectively as a formative feedback tool in large ESL writing classes when students are trained to use it. The author argues that its dialogic, immediate, and customizable feedback can support improvements in content, organization, and grammatical accuracy, with benefits sustained at delayed post-test. However, the study also notes constraints on generalizability because it was conducted at a single elite university, focused on only three writing genres, and involved a short intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with a comparison group, pre/post/delayed post testing, reported statistical assumptions, and sizable effects, but it is not a randomized K-12 trial and uses an intact higher-education sample with attrition from initial consent to analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported literacy effects are large, with very large within-group effect sizes and substantial post-test and delayed post-test differences favoring the ChatGPT condition. However, relevance to the target K-12 evidence question is indirect because the sample is undergraduate ESL students rather than school-age learners.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a formative feedback tool for self- and peer-assessment in an undergraduate ESL academic writing course, providing feedback on content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary during paragraph writing tasks.

Conversational use of ChatGPT to give dialogic, on-demand explanations and guidance during writing, including brainstorming, checking topic sentences, supporting details, conclusions, grammar, and vocabulary choices.

finding.finding_summary: In this quasi-experimental mixed-methods intervention, the ChatGPT group outperformed the comparison group on academic writing assessments after a 6-hour intervention and again at delayed post-test. Experimental-group scores increased from pre-test M=12.581 (SD=0.833, n=37) to post-test M=19.216 (SD=2.485) and delayed post-test M=20.419 (SD=2.575), with within-group RM ANOVA F(2,72)=330.704, p=5.146e-37, η²=0.902; Bonferroni comparisons showed very large gains from pre to post (d=3.300) and pre to delayed post (d=3.898), and a smaller continued gain from post to delayed post (d=0.598). Between groups, the experimental group exceeded the comparison group at post-test, t(70)=-5.643, p=3.297e-7, and delayed post-test, t(70)=-9.371, p=5.544e-14.
finding.measure: Rubric-scored academic writing tests on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph writing; rubric dimensions included content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
finding.study_size: n=72 analyzed total; experimental group n=37, comparison group n=35
finding.std_deviation: EG pre SD=0.833; EG post SD=2.485; EG delayed post SD=2.575; CG delayed post SD=1.897; CG post SD=1.695

finding.finding_summary: Focus group data indicated overwhelmingly positive student perceptions of ChatGPT’s impact, including increased motivation, reduced anxiety about asking for feedback, and greater confidence in obtaining immediate writing support. However, a minority of students reported concerns about reduced motivation to think independently and increased machine dependence, so the evidence is perception-based and somewhat mixed in nuance despite the overall positive direction.
finding.measure: Student focus group discussions on perceived motivation, anxiety reduction, and attitudes toward ChatGPT-supported feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT-supported self- and peer-assessment promoted learner autonomy, collaboration, and explicit reflection on writing decisions, especially around idea generation, organization, and grammar explanations. These findings come from qualitative coding rather than causal quantitative estimates, and some students also expressed concern that overreliance on the tool could dampen independent thinking and creativity.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes related to learner autonomy, collaboration, self-monitoring, and metalinguistic reflection

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative evidence suggests ChatGPT made brainstorming and feedback cycles faster, helped students complete writing tasks more efficiently, and was framed by the author as potentially useful in large classes where individualized feedback is difficult. These outcomes were not quantified experimentally, so the finding is based on user reports and author interpretation rather than measured time-on-task or workload reductions.
finding.measure: Focus group reports of faster writing, reduced brainstorming time, and perceived efficiency of feedback processes
